examples.title: A clean read
examples.text: Thirty-two pieces on a glossy vinyl board, seen at an angle. All 64 squares correct, on pieces as small as 25 pixels tall at the resolution the detector works in. It emitted 37 boxes here — the five that fall outside the predicted outline never reach the grid.

examples.title: One square, and it is a naming error
examples.text: The opening position after 1.b4 d5. Every piece is found, including the knight on b1 half hidden behind the rook — but from this angle it is called a rook too. That is the shape of almost every remaining error: the piece is seen, and then named wrongly.

examples.title: The back rank, where the tall pieces stand together
examples.text: Four wrong squares, all on the first rank: the queen on d1 is called a king, the bishop on f1 a queen, and the king and knight beside them are lost behind their neighbours. A crowded back rank seen from low down is the hardest thing on the board — queen-for-king is the single most common mistake in the whole split.

examples.title: Read from the wrong end
examples.text: The worst board in the split, and the pieces are not the problem: turn this answer around and it scores 64 of 64. Eight pieces on an almost empty board leave very little evidence for the last step, deciding which corner is a8, and it went the wrong way. Nothing else in 306 photographs is wrong by more than five squares.
